en: *Chanlin Baoxun*, Scroll One.
Compiled anew by the Śramaṇa Jingshan of Eastern Wu.
Master Mingjiao Song said: "There is nothing more venerable than the Way; there is nothing more beautiful than virtue. The Way..."
Where virtue resides,
even a commoner is not in distress;
where the Way and its Power do not reside, [even a noble is lost].
Though one may rule all under heaven, it is not the ultimate way.
Boyi and Shuqi were once men who starved to death;
yet now, we compare them with such a person.
Yet everyone rejoices.
Jie, Zhou, You, and Li were rulers of men in the past;
now, one compares them with those [present-day rulers].
Yet everyone becomes angry.
Therefore, those who study should worry that their Dao and Virtue are not fully embodied within themselves;
they should not worry that power and status do not reside with them. — *Xintan Ji* (Collected Works of Xintan).
Mingjiao said:
"The learning of the sages and worthies is certainly not something that can be mastered in a single day."
When the day is insufficient, it is followed by the night;
accumulated over months and years,
[the goal] can naturally be accomplished.
Therefore it is said:
"One studies to accumulate knowledge;
one questions to discern it."
This statement means that learning cannot be brought to illumination without the inquiry of debate.
Yet, among those who study today, it is rare for anyone to utter a single word of inquiry or debate with others.
One does not know how they will be able to assist in the development of the spiritual ground (*bhūmi*).
In the *Jiuping ji*, it says: "Mingjiao said,
'The Grand Historian read the *Mencius*.'"
Upon reaching the passage where King Hui of Liang asks, "How may I profit my state?
he involuntarily set down the scroll and sighed deeply: "Alas!"
Profit is the beginning of disorder;
therefore, the Master rarely spoke of profit,
constantly guarding its source.
The "original" refers to the beginning.
To honor the poor and lowly is the remedy for the弊 (evil) of craving profit.
How is this distinguished?
For those who serve the public,
if the pursuit of profit is not impartial, then the law will fall into disorder.
When those in private positions seek profit through deception, affairs fall into disorder.
When affairs are in disorder, people contend with one another in inequality.
When the law is in disorder, the people resent it and do not submit.
That which is rebellious, contentious,
and heedless of death and dying originates from this.
Is this not to say that profit is indeed the beginning of disorder?
Furthermore, the sages and worthies strictly cautioned against prioritizing profit and instead revered the primacy of benevolence and righteousness;
yet even in later generations, there were still those who relied upon profit to deceive one another.
How many have there been who have wounded the Way and subverted the teachings?
How much more so when one openly proclaims and practices a path for seeking profit?
If one wishes for the customs of the world to be upright rather than corrupt and base...
"Can this be found? In the *Xintan ji*. Mingjiao said:
'As for the evils committed by ordinary people...'"
There are those that have form and those that are formless.
Formless evils are those that harm people;
formed evils are those that kill people.
The evil of killing a person is small;
the evil of harming a person is great.
This is why there may be lethal poison amidst feasts and banquets.
Swords and spears lie within their laughter and conversation;
tigers and leopards dwell within their inner chambers;
barbarians and foreigners reside within their neighboring lanes.
Were it not for sages and worthies who cut it off before it has sprouted and guard against it through ritual and law,
its harm would be immense.
"Is this not indeed extreme? [asked] the *Wuxu Guangji*.
Mingjiao said, "The Venerable Dajue Liaan resided at Yuwang."
Because two monks were disputing over the distribution of offerings without ceasing,
the administrators were unable to resolve the matter.
Da Jue summoned them.
He rebuked him, saying:
"In the past, when Lord Bao presided over Kaifeng,
there was a citizen who came forward and said, 'I have lost a hundred taels of white gold that I entrusted to you.'"
Now he has returned to his home,
but his son will not accept it;
I hope that you, sir, will summon his son and cause him to return it.
The Duke sighed in wonder and immediately summoned his son to speak with him.
His son declined, saying,
"During my late father's lifetime..."
The Duke had privately sent some white silver to another room;
after the two men had firmly declined it for a long time,
the Duke could not help but yield.
The responsibility was entrusted to the temples and monasteries within the city to cultivate merit for the afterlife in order to offer it as a memorial for the deceased;
I witnessed this with my own eyes.
Furthermore, even those mired in the dust of worldly toil can thus disregard their wealth and admire righteousness;
yet you are a disciple of the Buddha.

Having no sense of integrity or shame such as this, he was subsequently expelled according to the monastic regulations of the forest-monasteries; thus it is recorded in the *Daguanji* (Records of the West Lake).
This refers to Master Da-jue Lian.
When he first traveled to Mount Lu,
Chan Master Neng of Yuan Tong saw him at once and regarded him as one of great capacity.
Someone asked, "By what means do you know this?
Nan replied, "This man is centered in the Mean and does not lean toward either side."
His deportment was dignified whether in motion or stillness;
moreover, his mastery of the Way and his conduct were exemplary,
and his speech was concise yet exhaustive in its principles.
Ordinary people with such endowments and capacities rarely fail to become accomplished masters. *Jiupeng ji* (Collected Works of Jiupeng),
early in the Renzong Huangyou era.
He dispatched a minor messenger with silver seals,
carrying a letter on green silk one chi in length,
to summon Yuan Tong-ne to reside at the Great Monastery of Xiaoci.
Nan declined to rise, citing illness.
He submitted a memorial stating that Da’jue should respond to the imperial summons.
Someone said:
The Sage Emperor honors and exalts virtue and morality;
his grace extends even to the springs and rocks.
Why does the Master so stubbornly decline?
Nan said, "I have unworthily joined the ranks of the monastic community,
and my hearing and sight are not keen."
I am fortunate to dwell in peace beneath the forest trees,
eating simple vegetables and drinking water;
though these are things even Buddhas and patriarchs would not have done.
How much more so for others?
As the ancient sages have said:
"It is difficult to dwell long beneath a great name."
Throughout my life, I have practiced the principle of contentment and have not allowed myself to be burdened by fame or profit.
If one’s heart is weary of these things, when will there ever be true sufficiency?
Thus Dongpo once said:
"To know contentment is honor;
to know sufficiency is wealth."
Avoiding fame to preserve one's integrity,
beginning well and ending well—
this is attained in the *Xing-shi* (Account of Conduct) of Yuan-tong.
Master Yuantong Ne said:
"The cripple's life depends on his staff;
were he to lose his staff, he would fall."
The life of a ferryman depends on his boat;
if he loses his boat, he will drown.
This applies to all those who dwell beneath the trees.
Those who have nothing to rely upon within themselves,
yet rely on external forces for their importance,
will lose everything the moment they are deprived of those external supports.
None can escape the calamity of falling or drowning—thus it is recorded in the *Lushan Yalu*.
Yuantong Ne said:
"In the past, the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang..."
He erected a forest of pillars, establishing them according to the rules of geometry,
desiring to remedy the corruption of the degenerate age;
yet he remained unaware that—
It is like scholars of the late age who steal the rules and regulations to destroy the monastic groves of Baizhang.
In the ancient world, although people lived in nests or caves, [the Way remained intact].
Everyone exercises self-restraint.
After attaining great wisdom,
even if one possesses high halls and spacious mansions, [one remains detached].
Everyone abandons themselves.
Therefore it is said:
"Safety and peril depend on virtue."
Rise and fall are matters of destiny.
If one’s virtue can sustain them,
why necessarily rely on monastic forests?
If numerical categories could indeed be relied upon,
why would one need the compass and square for recording the wild? Yuantong said to Dajue:
The ancient sages cultivated their minds before [afflictions] had sprouted and guarded their emotions before they were disordered;
for when one is prepared in advance, there will be no calamity.
Therefore, one sets up double gates and strikes the wooden clappers to await violent guests;
this is derived from the hexagram Yu (Preparation).
When affairs are prepared for in advance, they are easy to accomplish.
To ultimately achieve this is truly difficult.
Among the sages and philosophers of antiquity,
there were those who harbored lifelong anxieties.
That one may not suffer for even a single morning lies truly in this *Jiǔfēng jí* (The Collected Works of Jiǔfēng).
Master Dàjué Lián said:
Jade is not fashioned into a vessel unless it is carved;
a person does not know the Way unless they study.
What is known today is derived from what was known in antiquity.
The reason one knows what preceded through what followed is that the good may serve as a model,
while the evil may serve as a warning.
Observing those predecessors who established themselves and achieved renown in their time,
few did not accomplish this through learning. From the *Jiufeng ji*, Da Jue said:
The principle of the wondrous Way was once embodied by the sages in the *I Ching*. However,
when the Zhou dynasty declined, the laws of the former kings were destroyed and ritual propriety and righteousness perished.
Thereafter, strange words and heterodox arts appeared intermittently,
disrupting the customs of the people.
This continued until our Śākyamuni entered the Middle Kingdom.
He demonstrated the ultimate truth to people through his profound sincerity,
yet from beginning to end he established compassion as the means to transform all living beings.
This is also the means by which one accords with the times.
Since the birth of the people, when their primal simplicity had not yet dissipated, [the Way prevailed].
Thus, the teachings of the Three Sovereigns were simple and unadorned—
this was like spring. Yet, as the apertures of the emotions were daily excavated, [the world fell into decline].
The teachings of the Five Emperors were detailed and ornate;
this was the Xia period,
when the times and the world had changed.
Human sentiments change with the passing of days;
therefore, the teachings of the Three Kings were subtle yet rigorous,
like the autumn.
In the past, regarding the proclamations and oaths of the Shang and Zhou dynasties,
scholars of later generations were indeed unable to understand them.
If the people of that time listened to him without opposition,
how would their customs have differed from those of today?
When it reached its degeneration in the Qin and Han dynasties,
there was no limit to what they would do.
Thus, there were those in the world who could not bear to hear of it.
Thereupon, our Buddha, the Tathāgata,
once more expounded to him the principle of life and destiny,
saying: "It is winter."
Heaven has four seasons that circulate,
thereby generating and completing all things.
The sages established teachings to support one another in turn.
By means of this, one transforms and brings order to the world;
it is simply through this that it is accomplished.
Yet, when it reaches its ultimate limit—
None of them can avoid having their flaws;
these flaws are merely outward traces.
It must be that sages and worthies arise in the world from time to time to rescue them.
Since the Qin and Han dynasties, more than a thousand years have passed;
social customs have become increasingly decadent and thin.
Such is the teaching of the Sages.
They stand arrayed like tripods,
mutually reviling one another;
the Great Way lies desolate, with none returning to it.
Truly lamentable! This is from the letter to Minister Sun Xunlao.
Da Jue said: "Now, as one who presides over a particular region,"
If one wishes to practice the Way attained through realization and benefit others,
one must first subdue oneself, bestow kindness upon all things, and humble one's mind toward all beings;
only then will one regard gold and silk as mere refuse and soil.
"Then the fourfold assembly will honor and turn to him. [This was] from a letter to the Monk Xu of the Nine Immortals.
Da Jue said: "The elder possesses the potential for great intelligence."
They lacked any concern for their own safety or peril.
Those such as Shi Men Cong and Qi Xian Shun serve as examples from which one may take warning.
Thus, the fixed karma of human life is indeed difficult to discern clearly; yet,
if one examines its origins in detail, [it becomes evident].
How could one not know that this is the fault of negligence and lack of reflection?
Therefore it is said:
"Calamities lie hidden in the subtle and minute."
It arises from what people treat with negligence. Judging by this,
one should be especially cautious and reverent—
thus it is said in the *Jiupeng ji* (Collected Works of Nine Peaks).
Master Yunju Shun, whose courtesy name was Laofu,
resided at Qixian on Mount Lu.
Because the Governor of the Commandery, Hui, had harbored private resentment toward Du-guan and had unjustly stripped the people of their clothing,
he traveled to the capital to seek out Da-jue.
When I arrived at Chu Prefecture in Shanyang, I was detained by snow at an inn.
One night, a guest arrived with two servants, cutting through the snow;
upon seeing me, he regarded me as an old acquaintance.
Having changed his clothes, he prostrated himself before him.
The old man questioned him,
and the guest replied:
In the past, when I was at Dongshan following my master,
there was a man named Song Rong, a servant from Hanyang who carried my burdens;
I have conversed with this old man about our former days.
The guest sighed in admiration for a long time.
At dawn, he prepared a meal and presented him with five taels of white silver.
He then called for a servant.
The guest said,
"This boy has traveled to and from the capital several times."
"The hardships of the journey have been fully experienced;
you, Master, may proceed with confidence.
It is by virtue of this that I, an old man, have been able to reach the capital."
Inferring from this, one further understands the character these two men maintained throughout their lives (*Jiuping ji*). Da’jue said,
“The old man Shun was straightforward and simple by nature.”
He was ignorant of matters such as weights, measures, and commerce;
his daily routine remained constant and never changed.
Even tasks such as lighting lamps and sweeping the floor, he performed them all with his own hands.
He once said:
"The ancients had the precept that 'if one day one does not work, one shall not eat for that day.
What kind of person am I?"
Although he was advanced in years, his resolve became even firmer.
Someone asked:
"Why not employ attendants?"
The old man said,
"I have passed through both cold and heat,
and my rising and sitting have been irregular."
He did not wish to weary him.
Shun Laofu said, "Transmit and uphold this Way."
What is most precious is the complete truth:
to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox and eliminate deluded sentiments;
this is the true cultivation of the mind.
To clearly discern cause and effect regarding transgressions and blessings is the substance of one's conduct; it is through this that one propagates the Way and its Virtue.
To receive those who arrive from afar is the true duty of the abbot; having assessed their abilities,
he shall appoint them to administrative offices.
One thereby examines the reality of a person by observing their words and deeds to determine their suitability;
one thereby seeks the reality of the worthy.
They do not preserve the actual substance,
but merely parade empty fame;
this is of no benefit to principle.
Therefore, in a person’s conduct, sincerity alone is essential.

If one maintains this without wavering, then even amidst the level and the perilous, these two conditions can be unified; thus, both matters will be tranquil. — *Tanyuan-an Ji* (Collected Works from the Tranquil Hermitage).
Shun Laofu said to Master Fushan Yuan:
"If one wishes to investigate the unsurpassed, wondrous Way,
then in times of adversity one becomes even more resolute, and in old age one becomes even more vigorous."
One must not follow worldly custom to greedily steal fame and profit, thereby losing one's supreme virtue.
For jade is prized for its purity and luster;
thus, even vermilion and purple cannot alter its essential nature.
Beyond the pines lies the cold of winter;
frost and snow cannot wither their integrity.
Thus we know that integrity and righteousness are the greatest virtues under heaven.
"Your noble character is truly admirable;
how could you not exert yourself?
As the ancients said:"
With soaring wings he flies alone; his solitary wind has no companion.
It is only fitting that it should be so.
From the *Guanglu*: Master Fushan Yuan said:
The ancients served their teachers and chose their friends with such diligence that they did not dare to be remiss from dawn until dusk;
even when performing menial tasks such as tending the hearth or carrying grain for milling— sinking into lowly service— they never shied away from labor.
I have tested this repeatedly while stationed at Ye County.
However, as soon as there arises even the slightest thought of regarding profit and loss or weighing gain and loss,
one will resort to equivocation and indulgence to such an extent that nothing is left undone.
Furthermore, if one’s body is already not upright, how can one possibly study the Way? This was the Dharma-talk of Attendant Yue.
Master Yuan said:
Now, within the space between heaven and earth,
there are indeed things that grow easily;
suppose one were to expose them to the sun for a single day.
If one subjects it to cold for ten days,
there will likewise be none seen capable of bringing it to life.
Yet the unsurpassed, wondrous Way is brilliantly manifest within the space between one’s heart and mind.
Therefore, it is not difficult to perceive.
It depends primarily on the firmness of one's resolve and the vigor of one's practice;
it can be attained while sitting or standing.
If one believes for a single day but doubts for ten days,
or exerts oneself in the morning but grows weary by evening,
how could it be that [the truth] is merely difficult to perceive before one's eyes?
"I fear that I may spend my entire life turning my back on it," wrote Chan Master Yun.
Master Yuan Gong said:
"In the essentials of being an abbot, nothing takes precedence over discerning what to accept and what to reject."
The ultimate point of acceptance and rejection is determined within;
the sprouts of safety and peril are determined without.
Yet, safety is not the safety of a single day.
Danger is not the result of a single day;
it all arises from gradual accumulation and must be scrutinized.
Abide in the Way and its Virtue, and thereby accumulate the Way and its Virtue.
If one governs by means of ritual and righteousness, ritual and righteousness will accumulate;
if one governs by means of oppression and exploitation, resentment will accumulate.
When resentment accumulates, both those within and without will become alienated and turn away.
When ritual and righteousness accumulate, those both within and without become harmonious and joyful.
When the Way and its Virtue accumulate, those both within and without are moved and submit.
Therefore, when the Way, its Virtue, ritual, and righteousness are pervasive, those both within and without rejoice.
When the infliction of resentment reaches its extreme, both those within and without will lament.
Indeed, the response of calamity or fortune follows the stirrings of sorrow and joy.
Master Huiyuan said:
There are three essentials for maintaining the precepts:
benevolence and wisdom.
It is said: "Courageous.
The benevolent person practices the Way and its Virtue and promotes transformation and education.
He brings peace to those above and below and joy to those who come and go.
The wise person adheres to ritual and righteousness,
discerning safety and peril.
Examine the worthy and the foolish;
distinguish right from wrong.
The brave are decisive in their actions.
He will sever what is doubtful;
the treacherous shall surely be eliminated, and the sycophants shall surely be removed.
To be benevolent yet lacking clarity is like having fields that are not plowed;
to have clarity yet lack courage—
It is like having seedlings that are not weeded;
it is like being courageous but lacking benevolence,
or like reaping without knowing how to sow.
When these three are complete, the monastic community flourishes;
if one is lacking, it declines;
if two are lacking, it is in peril.
Third, if there were not even one [of these], then the way of maintaining the teachings would perish. [This was stated] in two documents sent to the Venerable Jingyin.
Master Yuan said:
The wise and the foolish, the virtuous and the unworthy,
are like water and fire that cannot share the same vessel,
or like cold and heat that do not coexist at the same time.
This is indeed their natural disposition.
The virtuous and wise are pure,
refined, upright, and profound.
They deliberate based on morality, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness;
in their speech and actions,
they only fear that these may not accord with human feelings or fail to penetrate the principles of things.
Those who are unworthy are treacherous,
perilous, deceitful, and sycophantic; they exalt themselves and display their own abilities,
while being addicted to desires and seeking only profit.
Disregarding everything else,
the Chan forest thus gained a worthy man whose virtue and conduct were cultivated.
The fundamental principles were established,
and thus the Dharma assembly was successfully formed;
even one unworthy person found a place among them.
He stirs up the masses and brings disorder to both the inner and outer realms, leaving all in a state of unease.
Though he possesses great wisdom, what use is his knowledge of ritual and law?
Such is the difference between the wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy, the superior and the inferior.
How could one not exercise discernment? A letter from the Venerable Huili Fang.
Master Yuan said:
"The abbot occupies the superior position."
One should receive those below with humility;
when serving those in subordinate positions,
one must serve those above with complete sincerity.
When those above and below are in harmony,
the way of maintaining the community will flow unimpeded. Yet,
those who occupy superior positions often become arrogant and self-important.
If those below are negligent and become estranged from themselves,
and the relationship between superiors and subordinates fails to flow,
then the Way of the Abbot will be blocked.
When the ancient worthies resided as abbots, they were at leisure and free from affairs;
they would engage in relaxed discussions with their students on all manner of topics.
Consequently, a single word or half-verse from them has been recorded in biographies and is still praised to this day.
What is the reason for this?
First, it is because one wishes to ensure that the sentiments of those above are communicated to those below,
so that the Way remains free from obstruction or concealment.
Second, he can foreknow whether a student’s talent and capacity are sufficient;
thus, in all matters of advancement or withdrawal, he acts with perfect appropriateness.
Naturally, those above and below are harmonious and reverent, and those far and near are drawn toward him with respect.
"The flourishing of the monastic communities (conglin) is brought about by this," [as stated] in the letter to Master Qing Huayan.
Master Yuan said to Daowu Zhen:
"If one's study has not yet reached the Way..."
Those who flaunt their learning and见闻 (jìnwén),
racing about with their intellectual acumen and seeking to triumph through the sharpness of their eloquence,
are like a latrine smeared with vermilion and lacquer.
It merely increases its stench. From the *Xihu Jiwen*:
Master Yuan told Chan Master Yan, "The mind is the master of the body."
The root of the myriad practices is the mind;
if it does not attain subtle awakening, deluded emotions arise spontaneously.
Once deluded emotions have arisen, one’s vision of principle remains obscure.
When the vision of principle is not clear, right and wrong become confused;
therefore, in governing the mind, one must seek wondrous awakening.
Upon awakening, the spirit becomes harmonious and the vital energy tranquil.
With a composed countenance and dignified bearing,
all delusive thoughts and mental anxieties are melted away into the true mind.
By using this to govern the mind, the mind itself becomes spontaneously spiritual and wondrous.
Thereafter, who would not follow his transformation as he guided beings and pointed out their delusions? From the *Fushan Shilu*:
Master Wuzu Yan said, "In these times, among those in the monastic communities who study the Way..."
That one's reputation does not spread and that one is not trusted by others is because their brahmacarya is not pure.
In their conduct as persons, they lack sincerity and integrity;
they often seek fame, reputation, profit, and offerings through expedient means,
even going so far as to ostentatiously display their outward ornaments.
Consequently, they were censured by those with discernment;
thus, they obscured the essential subtlety [of the teaching].
Even if one possesses the Way and Virtue like that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, [one will be disparaged].
Having heard and seen this, you may harbor doubts and fail to believe it.
On a future day, when you yourselves have taken up a thatch-roofed hut [to dwell as monks],
you should encourage yourselves by means of this letter from Fojian to Foguo.
The Patriarch Yan said:
"When my late master first resided at Yangqi,
it was an old house with dilapidated rafters that barely shielded him from wind and rain."
Just as winter approached its end,
snow and sleet filled my bed;
I had no leisure even to remain in my dwelling.
A patch-robed monk came forward with sincere devotion, wishing to serve as a laborer for the construction project.
The Master, however, declined him, saying:
"The Buddha has said:"
At such a time, the kalpa is in decline;
high cliffs and deep valleys undergo constant change and transformation.
How could one find permanence, fulfillment, or the attainment of one's desires through self-seeking contentment?
You have left the household life to study the Way,
yet your practice remains unsteady;
already you are forty or fifty years of age.
"How could there be leisure to concern oneself with grand buildings?
He ultimately did not comply.
The next day, he ascended the hall and said:
"Yangqi has newly settled in; the walls of the house are thin.
The entire bed is strewn with pearls of snow."
He shrinks his neck and sighs in silent lamentation;
he turns his thoughts back to the ancients who dwelt beneath the trees— thus it is recorded in the *Guanglu*.
The Patriarch said:
"A patch-robed monk guards the city of the mind and upholds the precepts."
Reflect upon it day and night;
practice it morning and evening.
In your practice, let nothing exceed your reflection.
Thoughts that do not transcend proper conduct have their beginning and bring their end to fruition,
just as a plowman has his boundaries.
"His transgressions were few indeed.
Chan Master Yanzu said:
"That which is called a 'congregation' (conglin)..."
It is the place where the holy and the ordinary are forged and refined, and where talents and characters are nurtured;
it is from here that transformation and education emerge. Although beings dwell together in groups and gather in classes, [it is here they find their true purpose].
They were led and brought into alignment,
each having its own lineage of teachers.
Now, however, those in various regions do not strive to maintain the laws and regulations of the former sages.
With their biased emotions of liking and disliking, they mostly transform others by asserting their own correctness;
how then can later generations take them as models? These two matters are clearly gathered here.
The Patriarch Yan said:
"In propagating the Way and benefiting sentient beings, the essential task lies in finding the right person;
yet the difficulty of knowing people has been a source of concern even for the sages and philosophers."
One may listen to their words yet not guarantee their conduct;
one may seek their conduct yet fear overlooking their talent.
Unless one has previously associated with them and possesses full knowledge of their background from beginning to end, [one cannot judge them].
By investigating their aspirations and conduct, and observing their capacities and abilities,
one can then come to know those who preserve the Way and conceal their talents.
Those who purchase fame and polish their outward appearance cannot conceal their hypocrisy;
even if they remain hidden and secret, their origins will eventually be revealed.
Now, the principle of observing, investigating, examining,
and listening is certainly not something that can be mastered in a single morning or evening;
this is why after Nanyue Huairang met Dajian Huineng, [he remained for many years].
It has been fifteen autumns since you took up these duties. When Mazu saw Xuanzang,
he also followed him for over ten years.
Thus we know that at the moment of transmission between the former sages,
it was certainly not something that those of shallow capacity dared to uphold;
it was like water being passed from one vessel to another.
Only then can one truly succeed to the grand legacy,
like a weed growing from its own kind;
this is the clear verification of the principle of observation, investigation, and detailed listening.

"How could those who employ clever words and artful countenances, or who are fawning, sycophantic, and obsequious, ever be permitted to fill these selections? Thus spoke Yuanwu in his letter to Master Yan. Yuanwu said:
The great handle for maintaining the monastic community rests upon both benevolence and virtue; it is impossible to neglect either.
If one possesses benevolence but lacks virtue, people will not respect them.
If one possesses virtue but offers no kindness, people will not feel affection for them.
If one knows that kindness can evoke affection,
they should augment their virtue to complement it.
Thus, the grace thus bestowed is sufficient to bring peace to those above and below and to guide those from the four quarters;
provided that one knows virtue is worthy of reverence.
If one adds the grace of mutual assistance,
then the virtue one maintains will be sufficient to continue the legacy of those who attained awakening first and to guide the ignorant and deluded.
Therefore, one who abides well in upholding [the Dharma] nurtures virtue to practice benevolence,
and proclaims benevolence to maintain virtue.
If one possesses virtue and is able to nourish others, they will not be diminished;
if one possesses kindness and is able to act upon it, there will be grace.
Thus, virtue and kindness accumulate one another.
When wisdom and virtue are practiced in tandem,
then virtue need not be cultivated through effort, yet one’s reverence will equal that for the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
wisdom need not be exerted with toil, yet one’s affection will be like that for one's parents.
Thus, among those throughout the lakes and seas who possess the aspiration for the Way,
who would not come to take refuge here?
As the abbot transmits the Way and its Virtue to promote teaching and transformation, [all shall gather].
Not understanding this essential point, they fail to attain it; thus [Yunmen] wrote to Foyan.
